clinicalPearls: A benign disorder of infancy defined by a triad of fine rapid asymmetric nystagmus, head nodding and an anomalous head posture
The nystagmus is typically small-amplitude, high-frequency and often dissociated or intermittent between the two eyes
Onset is usually in the first year of life and the condition tends to resolve spontaneously within a few years
It is a diagnosis of exclusion because chiasmal and suprasellar tumours (such as optic pathway gliomas) can mimic it
Neuroimaging is mandatory to exclude an intracranial lesion before accepting a benign diagnosis
Retinal dystrophies can produce similar nystagmus and may need electrophysiological testing to exclude
reference.pathophysiology: Spasmus nutans is an idiopathic, usually self-limiting disorder of ocular motor control in infancy of unknown mechanism, in which the head nodding is thought to be a partially compensatory response to the shimmering nystagmus. Because an identical clinical picture can be produced by anterior visual pathway tumours compressing the chiasm and by certain retinal dystrophies, the benign form can only be diagnosed once these structural and retinal causes have been excluded.
additionalDifferentials: Acquired nystagmus from posterior fossa disease
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain and anterior visual pathways
Electroretinography where a retinal dystrophy is suspected
redFlags: Optic disc pallor or afferent pupillary defect
Failure to resolve or progression of signs
Associated neurological deficit or failure to thrive
Monocular or grossly asymmetric visual loss
reference.prognosis: The idiopathic form is benign and usually resolves spontaneously over months to a few years; prognosis otherwise depends entirely on excluding and, if present, treating a structural or retinal cause.
pitfalls: Accepting the diagnosis without neuroimaging and missing an optic pathway glioma
Overlooking a retinal dystrophy as the cause of the nystagmus
Confusing it with congenital nystagmus syndrome
Attributing the head nodding to a primary movement disorder
references: Taylor and Hoyt's Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
management: Mandatory neuroimaging with MRI of the brain and anterior visual pathways to exclude a chiasmal or suprasellar tumour before accepting a benign diagnosis
Electroretinography where a retinal dystrophy is suspected as a mimic
Once structural and retinal causes are excluded, manage conservatively with reassurance as the condition is self-limiting
Regular ophthalmological and orthoptic follow-up to monitor the nystagmus, head posture and visual development
Developmental and neurological review to confirm normal progress
Refer promptly for treatment of any underlying lesion if imaging identifies a structural or retinal cause
